entry: Branch of [[Topology|topology]] concerned with mathematical knots. A mathematical knot is a loop whose ends are joined so that it cannot be undone, formally an embedding of a circle in three-dimensional [[Euclidean space]]. Two knots are equivalent if one can be deformed into the other without cutting the string or passing it through itself. A fundamental problem is determining when two descriptions, such as knot diagrams, represent the same knot. Knots are distinguished by invariants, quantities that remain the same for all descriptions of a knot, including knot polynomials, knot groups and hyperbolic invariants. In the 1860s, [[Lord Kelvin]]'s theory that atoms were knots in the aether led Peter Guthrie Tait to create the first knot tables. More than six billion knots and links have been tabulated since the 19th century.

Unit of speed equal to one [[Nautical mile|nautical mile]] per hour, exactly 1.852 km/h (about 1.151 mph or 0.514 m/s). The ISO symbol is kn, though kt is common in [[Aviation|aviation]], where the International Civil Aviation Organization recommends it. The knot is a non-SI unit used in meteorology and in maritime and air navigation. The name derives from the chip log, a line with knots tied at intervals that was used to measure ship speed until the mid-19th century.

City in eastern Tennessee, county seat of Knox County (pop., 2020: 190,740), on the Tennessee River in the [[Appalachian Mountains]]. It was the first capital of Tennessee and grew into a major wholesaling and manufacturing center after the [[American Civil War]]. The [[Great Depression]] brought the collapse of its manufacturing sector. The 1982 World's Fair helped revitalize the city. It is home to the flagship campus of the University of Tennessee and is a gateway to the [[Great Smoky Mountains National Park]].

Norwegian novelist and playwright. He was awarded the 1920 [[Nobel Prize]] in Literature for *Growth of the Soil*. He pioneered psychological literature using stream of consciousness and interior monologue, influencing [[Thomas Mann]], [[Franz Kafka]], [[Hermann Hesse]] and Ernest Hemingway. His early works, such as *Hunger* (1890), are associated with the Neo-Romantic revolt against realism and naturalism; his later Nordland novels portray everyday life in rural [[Norway]]. He openly supported [[Adolf Hitler]] and [[Nazi Germany]], met Hitler during the German occupation of Norway, and donated his Nobel medal to [[Joseph Goebbels]]. Charged with treason after the war, he was not convicted but was fined in 1948. His last book, *On Overgrown Paths*, was written during semi-imprisonment and concerned his postwar treatment.

Arboreal herbivorous [[Marsupial|marsupial]] native to Australia. Its closest living relatives are [[Wombat|wombats]]. Koalas live in open [[Eucalyptus]] woodland, whose leaves make up most of their diet; the eucalypt diet has low nutritional and caloric content and contains toxic compounds. Koalas are largely sedentary and sleep up to twenty hours a day. Koalas give birth to young called joeys, which live in the mother's pouch for their first six to seven months. The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists the species as vulnerable, but in February 2022 it was listed as endangered in the Australian Capital Territory, [[New South Wales]] and [[Queensland]]. Koalas are over-abundant in parts of [[South Australia]] and [[Victoria (state)|Victoria]]. Along with [[Kangaroo|kangaroos]], koalas are a worldwide symbol of Australia.

City, capital of Hyōgo Prefecture, [[Japan]]. It lies on the north shore of Osaka Bay about 35 km (22 mi) west of [[Osaka]] and is Japan's third-largest port city after [[Tokyo]] and Yokohama. It was one of the cities opened to trade with the West after 1853 and retains a rich architectural heritage from the Meiji era. The modern city was founded in 1889 and became a designated city in 1956. The 1995 Great Hanshin earthquake diminished some of its prominence as a port city, but it remains Japan's fourth-busiest container port. Companies headquartered there include ASICS and Kawasaki Heavy Industries, and the city is the point of origin and namesake of Kobe beef.

American basketball player nicknamed the Black Mamba. He played his entire 20-year career with the [[Los Angeles Lakers]], winning five [[National Basketball Association|NBA]] championships. He was named 2008 NBA Most Valuable Player and scored a career-high 81 points on January 22, 2006. In 2003 he was charged with sexual assault; the criminal charges were dismissed, and he settled a related lawsuit out of court while maintaining that the encounter was consensual. He was killed in a helicopter crash in Calabasas, California, along with eight others.

Port city (pop., 2011: 677,381) on the Malabar Coast of [[Kerala]], India. It is the state's financial and industrial capital and was a spice-trading center from antiquity. The construction of Cochin [[Port|port]] and the reclamation of Willingdon Island in 1928 transformed it into a major seaport. It is home to Cochin Shipyard, India's largest [[Shipbuilding|shipbuilding]] and maintenance facility by capacity, and has hosted India's first art biennale, the Kochi-Muziris Biennale, since 2012. Cochin International Airport is the first in the world to operate solely on [[Solar energy|solar energy]].

[[Brown bear]] subspecies (*Ursus arctos middendorffi*) of the Kodiak Archipelago, [[Alaska]]. Together with the [[Polar bear]], it is one of the two largest kinds of bears alive. Kodiak bears are on average 1.5 to 2 times larger than mainland [[Grizzly bear|grizzly]] bears, but their diet and lifestyle differ little from other brown bears. Genetically isolated since at least the last ice age, the population has very little genetic diversity. The Alaska Department of Fish and Game closely monitors the population and the number of bears hunted in the state.

Ghanaian diplomat, seventh secretary-general of the [[United Nations]] (1997–2006). He was born in [[Kumasi]], Ghana, and joined the United Nations in 1962, working for the [[World Health Organization]] in [[Geneva]]. He was the first secretary-general chosen from the UN's own staff. As secretary-general he reformed the UN bureaucracy, worked to combat [[HIV/AIDS]], and launched the UN Global Compact. He was criticized for not expanding the Security Council and faced calls to resign after the Oil-for-Food Programme investigation, but was largely exonerated of personal corruption. In 2012 he became joint UN–Arab League special representative for Syria but quit, frustrated by the lack of progress in resolving the [[Syrian civil war]]. After his term he founded the Kofi Annan Foundation in 2007 to work on international development.

Biennial vegetable, a stout cultivar of wild cabbage (*Brassica oleracea*). The swollen stem is the most frequently used edible part, eaten raw in salads and slaws or cooked. Its taste resembles a [[Broccoli|broccoli]] stem or [[Cabbage|cabbage]] heart, but it is milder and sweeter. Created by artificial selection, it shares its species with cabbage, broccoli, [[Kale|kale]] and [[Brussels sprout|Brussels sprouts]]. Its name combines *Kohl* (cabbage) and *Rübe* (turnip). The first European written record dates to 1554. Per 100 g, raw kohlrabi supplies 27 calories and 65% of the Daily Value for vitamin C. Its leaves can be cooked like collard greens or kale. It flowers and sets seed in its second year.

Colored ornamental variety of [[Carp|carp]], also called *nishikigoi* (brocaded carp). They are kept in outdoor ponds and water gardens. Systematic breeding for color and pattern began in Niigata, [[Japan]], in the early 19th century. Varieties are distinguished by coloration, patterning and scalation, with colors including white, black, red, orange, yellow, blue, brown and cream, and metallic gold and silver-white. The most popular category is the Gosanke, made up of the Kōhaku, Taishō Sanshoku and Shōwa Sanshoku varieties. Over 100 varieties exist today, and koi can live over 70 years under optimal conditions. When released into non-native waterways, koi become an [[Invasive species|invasive species]]; their bottom-feeding increases turbidity and displaces native fish.

Early 8th-century Japanese chronicle of [[Myth|myths]] and genealogies. According to its preface, Ō no Yasumaro compiled it at the request of Empress Genmei and presented it in 712. It is usually considered the oldest extant literary work in [[Japan]]. Written in [[Classical Chinese]], it includes songs in Old Japanese transcribed phonetically, and draws on [[Oral tradition|oral traditions]] and clan records. Its narrative establishes the imperial Yamato line's right to rule, portraying it as descended from heavenly deities. Together with the *Nihon Shoki*, it helped inspire many practices and a unified [[Shinto]] orthodoxy, and its myths were later incorporated into Shinto practices such as the misogi purification ritual.

City, capital of [[West Bengal]], [[India]], on the eastern bank of the Hooghly River. After a 1690 trading license from the Nawab of Bengal, the [[East India Company]] developed the area into Fort William. As the de facto capital of India until 1911, Calcutta (its official name until 2001) was the second largest city in the [[British Empire]] after London. It was associated with the Bengali Renaissance and was the hotbed of the Indian nationalist movement. Overtaken by [[Mumbai]] as India's largest city, it hosted the government-in-exile of [[Bangladesh]] during the [[Bangladesh Liberation War]] in 1971. It is the center of the Indian Bengali film industry, Tollywood, and is known for [[Durga]] Puja, a Hindu festival recognized by UNESCO.

Fermented, effervescent, sweetened [[Black tea|black tea]] drink. Made by [[Fermentation|fermenting]] tea with a symbiotic culture of bacteria and [[Yeast|yeast]] (SCOBY), often called a mother. Commercial versions contain small amounts of alcohol. It is believed to have originated in [[China]] and had spread to Russia and Eastern Europe by the early 20th century. Its global market was worth approximately US$1.7 billion as of 2019. Numerous health benefits have been claimed, but there is little evidence for them, and the drink is not recommended for therapeutic purposes.

[[Monitor lizard]] (*Varanus komodoensis*), the largest living lizard species. Endemic to a few small [[Indonesia|Indonesian]] islands, including Komodo and Rinca, it is an [[Apex predator|apex predator]] that dominates its ecosystems. Males grow to a maximum length of 3 m (10 ft) and weigh up to 150 kg (330 lb). Adults hunt large [[Mammal|mammals]], mainly Javan rusa and feral pigs, and also eat considerable amounts of carrion. Young dwell in trees to avoid predators, including cannibalistic adults, and take 8 to 11 years to mature. Mating begins between May and August, and as many as 20 eggs are laid in September and incubated for seven to eight months. The IUCN lists the species as endangered, and Komodo National Park was founded in 1980 to aid its protection. It is protected under Indonesian law.

Last royal dynasty of Burma, 1752–1885, also called the Third Burmese Empire. The dynasty was founded in 1752 by a village chief, later known as [[Alaungpaya]], who by 1759 had reunited Burma. Its kings expanded the realm into the second-largest empire in Burmese history, taking [[Assam]] and [[Manipur]] and sacking Ayutthaya in Siam in 1767. The dynasty fought four wars successfully against the [[Qing dynasty]] of China and later restored trade with it. The [[British Empire]] defeated the Burmese in three Anglo-Burmese Wars between 1824 and 1885 and ended the monarchy in 1885. The capital was moved several times, and Mindon (reigned 1853–1878) relocated it to [[Mandalay]].

German statesman, first chancellor of [[West Germany]] (1949–1963). A devout Catholic, he was mayor of [[Cologne]] from 1917 to 1933 and a leading politician of the Catholic Center Party in the [[Weimar Republic]]. As the first leader of the Christian Democratic Union (1946–1966), he worked to restore the West German economy under a market-based system and liberal democracy. A strong anti-communist with an Atlanticist foreign policy, he brought West Germany into [[NATO]] and helped reestablish its armed forces (the Bundeswehr) and intelligence services in 1955 and 1956. He refused diplomatic recognition of [[East Germany]] and of the Oder–Neisse line as [[Poland|Poland]]'s postwar frontier. A proponent of [[European integration]], he signed the Treaty of Rome in 1957.

Austrian zoologist and ethologist. He shared the 1973 [[Nobel Prize]] in Physiology or Medicine with Nikolaas Tinbergen and Karl von Frisch. Regarded as a founder of modern [[Ethology|ethology]], the study of animal behavior, he is known for his descriptions of imprinting in greylag geese, in which young birds bond instinctively with the first moving object they see. In 1936 he met Tinbergen, and the two collaborated in developing ethology as a separate sub-discipline of [[Biology|biology]]. Lorenz was recruited into the German Army as a medic in 1941 and was sent to the [[Eastern Front (World War II)|Eastern Front]] in 1944. He was captured by the [[Red Army]] and spent four years as a prisoner of war in Soviet Armenia. He had been a member of the [[Nazi Party]] and later regretted it. His popular books include *King Solomon's Ring*, *On Aggression* and *Man Meets Dog*.

German civil engineer and pioneering computer scientist. He built the Z3, which became operational in May 1941 and was the world's first functional programmable computer. Zuse developed the Z1 in his parents' apartment in Berlin, and it was destroyed in 1944 in a British air raid. After 1939 the government of Nazi Germany provided him resources, and his Z2 used telephone [[Relay|relays]]. In 1941 he founded a company that produced the Z4, which became the world's first commercial computer. From 1943 to 1945 he designed Plankalkül, the first high-level programming language. [[IBM]] took an option on his patents in 1946. After [[World War II]] he established Zuse KG in 1949, producing commercial computers.

Russian and Soviet actor and theater director. He co-founded the Moscow Art Theatre with Vladimir Nemirovich-Danchenko and promoted the new Russian drama of [[Anton Chekhov]], [[Maxim Gorky]] and Mikhail Bulgakov. The company's productions of *The Seagull* (1898) and *Hamlet* (1911–12) established his reputation. His principal fame rests on his [[System|system]] of actor training, preparation and rehearsal technique, which grew out of a crisis in 1906. He was formative in the development of Vsevolod Meyerhold and other practitioners. A heart attack on stage in 1928 ended his acting career, though he continued to direct, teach and write until his death. His acting manual *An Actor's Work* appeared posthumously in 1938. His autobiography, *My Life in Art*, is not always accurate about his artistic development.

Genus of terrestrial tree [[Kingfisher|kingfishers]] native to [[Australia]] and [[New Guinea]]. The name, from the Wiradjuri *guuguubarra*, imitates its call. The loud call of the laughing kookaburra is a stock sound effect for Australian bush or jungle settings in older movies. Kookaburras are almost exclusively carnivorous, eating lizards, snakes, frogs, rodents, beetles and the young of other birds. They wait on powerlines or low branches, dive on prey and bash larger prey against a tree or the ground. Five species of kookaburra occur in Australia, New Guinea and the Aru Islands.

Sea passage between the Korean Peninsula and [[Japan]]. It connects the [[East China Sea]], the [[Yellow Sea]] and the [[Sea of Japan]] in the northwest Pacific Ocean. The strait is about 200 km (120 mi) wide, and Tsushima Island divides it into a western channel and the Tsushima Strait. Many international shipping lanes pass through it, and Japan and [[South Korea]] have limited their territorial claims there to 3 nautical miles (5.6 km), allowing free passage. The strait was the site of the 1950 Battle of Korea Strait during the [[Korean War]]. A joint Mongol-Korean fleet crossed it in 1274 and 1281 in attempts to invade Japan, and Buddhism reached Japan over the strait in the 6th century. A warm branch of the Kuroshio Current, the Tsushima Current, passes through it. A tunnel under the strait, the Japan–Korea Undersea Tunnel, has been proposed.

Peninsular region in East Asia, including Jeju Island and smaller islands. Since 1945 it has been divided at or near the 38th parallel into [[North Korea]] and [[South Korea]], both established in 1948. The [[Korean War]] (1950–1953) ended in stalemate without a peace treaty, and a demilitarized zone approximates the original partition. In 668, Silla conquered Baekje and Goguryeo with the aid of the [[Tang dynasty]]. [[Goryeo]], whose name gave rise to the English word Korea, ruled a unified peninsula until the [[Joseon]] dynasty was founded in 1392. Japan annexed the peninsula in 1910, and [[Korea under Japanese rule|colonial rule]] lasted until Japan's surrender in 1945. South Korea is a developed country and the world's fourteenth-largest economy by GDP (PPP), and its pop culture, notably [[K-pop]], has global influence. North Korea follows Songun, a military-first policy, and many observers consider its human rights record the worst in the world.

Colonial period, 1910–1945, under the [[Empire of Japan]]. Japan annexed Korea in 1910 and ruled it as a colony named Chōsen. Japan built railways, ports and roads, but many workers faced poor conditions and discriminatory pay. Japan pursued Japanization, banning Korean names and the Korean language. From 1939 Japan mobilized about 5.4 million Koreans for its war effort, and many women were forced into sexual slavery as [[Comfort women|comfort women]]. After [[Surrender of Japan|Japan's surrender]] in 1945, the peninsula was divided into Soviet and American zones, leading to two states in 1948. Its legacy remains contested in [[South Korea]] and Japan.
